layout_dets.text: Susceptibility of Cr-Ni-Mn Stainless Steels to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pitting in Chloride Solutions*

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: E. LUNARSKA, Z. SZKLARSKA-SMIALOWSKA, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: M. JANIK-CZACHOR*

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abstract

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Anodic behavior of 18Cr-5Ni steels containing 0.03 to 15% Mn was studied in 0.1N

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with additions of 0.01 to 0.1N NaCl. The presence of 5.7 to 15% Mn in those steels decreases their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ability to passivate and their resistance to pitting. The most susceptible locations for pit nucleation are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boundaries between the austenite matrix and the carbide particles. The pitting resistance of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chromium-nickel-manganese steels is discussed with respect to their phase compositions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Only a scarcity of information on the susceptibility of Cr-Ni-Mn

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steels to pitting exists in the literature, and the few existing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data are controversial. This is chiefly due to the fact that these steels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are extremely sensitive to the presence of minor components,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particularly nitrogen. Researchers have not paid sufficient respect to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this element. Thus, Murgulescu and Radovici¹ studied the anodic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: behavior of steels with 17 to 19% Cr, 5 to 7% Ni, and 4.4 to 7.7%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mn, and found a detrimental effect of increasing Mn content on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ability of these steels to passivate. On the other hand, Knyazheva, et

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: observed that addition of up to 10% Mn to 18%Cr-5%Ni

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steels does not affect the passive dissolution rate in sulfuric acid

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solutions, but increases the critical current density and the critical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passivation potential. Unfortunately, in both papers, the nitrogen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: content was not indicated.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Condylis, et al,³ compared the corrosion resistance of 304L and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 316L austenitic stainless steels with that of substitutional 204L and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 216L steels containing about 6% Ni, 10% Mn, and 0.2% N. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: substitutional low-nickel steels behaved like the ordinary austenitic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steels in many solutions. The important exception was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nitric acid. In that solution, the manganese steels were less resistant.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In chloride solutions, the pitting resistance of Mn-containing steels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was higher than that of 304L and 316L steels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: According to Shams El Din, et al,4 who investigated the anodic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: behavior of 17Cr-5Ni steels containing from 0.03 to 13.9% Mn, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion behavior of the 17Cr-5Ni-5.6Mn alloy approaches that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 18Cr-8Ni steel. However, a further increase in the Mn content is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: detrimental to both the corrosion resistance and ability to passivate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In a subsequent paper,⁵ these authors argue that additions of Mn to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 17Cr-5Ni alloys adversely affect their pitting resistance. On the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contrary, the experimental results of Troselius6 suggest that Mn

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: addition to Cr-Ni steels has a beneficial influence on the pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resistance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: When considering the effect of Mn on the corrosion resistance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of stainless steels, it must be taken into account that the change in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the chemical composition might be accompanied by a change in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phase composition of the alloy. This change could significantly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affect the mechanical and chemical properties. In this respect, minor

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elements and impurities (C,N,P) play a role as important as that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cr, Ni, and Mn.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The purpose of the present work was to study the effect of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different additions of Mn to the 18Cr-5Ni alloy on the phase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: composition and susceptibility to pitting in chloride solutions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Our results show that the presence of 5.7 to 15% Mn in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 18Cr-5Ni steels adversely affects their ability tò passivate and their

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resistance to pitting (Figures 3-5). This harmful effect increases with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increasing Cl concentration in the electrolyte. The effect is greater

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for steels in the as-received condition, i.e., hot forged steels, than in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quenched steels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A decrease of the corrosion resistance of 18Cr-5Ni-Mn steels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relative to the 18Cr-8Ni austenitic stainless steels cannot be ascribed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the presence of the δ-phase (δ-ferrite) in the alloys under

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: investigation. This conclusion is based on the following arguments:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (1) the relatively high corrosion resistance and ease of passivation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the martensitic-ferritic steel, (2) the corrosion immunity of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: δ-phase in quenched alloys, and (3) the similar shapes of the anodic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: polarization curves for quenched alloys containing 9.6% Mn and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 10% Mn, despite their different phase compositions. The 10% Mn

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloy contained much more δ-ferrite than the other alloy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Suggestion can be made that in ternary Cr-Ni-Mn alloys

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compared with ordinary Cr-Ni stainless steels, the austenite has a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lower ability to be passivated anodically in chloride solutions, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: forms weaker passive films.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As revealed by metallographic examination, the most suscep-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tible locations for pit nucleation in quenched steels are the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boundaries between the γ-phase and carbide particles.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is nearly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equal for both the hot-forged and quenched alloys. This suggests

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that in both cases the most susceptible locations for pit nucleation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are the same. In hot forged steels, fine carbide precipitations were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: observed at γ-δ-boundaries, as well as within the δ-phase itself

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Figure 7). These precipitates form during hot forging or slow

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cooling as a result of the δ-phase degradation. The relatively higher

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosiveness of the δ-phase in the as-received alloys was most likely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: due to those carbide precipitates.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Conclusions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1. Addition of 5.7 to 15% Mn to 18Cr-5Ni steels diminishes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: their ability to be passivated and their resistance to pitting.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. The most susceptible locations for pit nucleation in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quenched steels are the boundaries between the γ-phase and carbide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particles.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3. The presence of the δ-phase in the steels does not affect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting susceptibility.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Properties of Titanium-Cadmium Deposit*

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: DAN ALTURA* and FLORIAN MANSFELD**

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abstract

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Titanium-cadmium plating was evaluated at various plating current densities which may be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encountered in industrial practice. Both high and low current densities resulted in increased hydrogen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: embrittlement tendency over the optimal plating condition. Deleting the current strike had no

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: noticeable effect on embrittlement behavior. Salt spray testing indicated that gross corrosion behavior

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was independent of plating current density. The corrosion behavior of cadmium-plated steel coupled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to aluminum alloys was both a function of plating current density and the type of aluminum alloy

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used. Plate microstructure was a strong function of plating current density.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The addition of titanium compounds to a cadmium-cyanide plating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bath was originally suggested as a means of improving the corrosion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resistance of the resultant cadmium plate. Subsequently it was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: discovered that the addition of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (pertitanate) to the cadmium-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cyanide bath significantly reduces the amount of hydrogen absorbed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: codeposition of titanium with the cadmium, resulting in a change in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the structure of the deposit which guards against the entry of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In order to further reduce the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: embrittling tendency of this cyanide bath, the use of organic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: brighteners has been eliminated. The lower embrittlement tendency

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the titanium-cadmium (Ti-Cd) plating bath has made it an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effective replacement for the bright cyanide bath in the plating of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high-strength steels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hydrogen into the steel.3,5

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Optimal operation of the Ti-Cd plating bath requires tight

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: control of plating bath parameters. Chemical composition of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bath is controlled through periodic chemical analysis of such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: important bath constituents as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cd, and cyanide. One plating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parameter which is difficult to control effectively and can some-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: times fall outside the optimal range is local plating current density.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The plating current density at edges or other projections can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: significantly greater than the nominal value, while in voids the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: current density can be smaller than the nominal. This study was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: initiated to investigate the effect of plating current density on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performance of the Ti-Cd bath. Bath performance was evaluated in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: terms of hydrogen embrittlement tendency of the steel substrate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and corrosion behavior of the deposit.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Experimental Procedure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Plating solutions contained 15 oz/gal (112 g/l) sodium cyanide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and 3.4 oz/gal (25.4 g/l) CdO. Titanium content of the plating

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solution was controlled by using atomic absorption analysis.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Temperature of the bath was maintained at 21 (± 3) C. Cadmium

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: balls were the anodes. Plating current densities which were studied

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are given in Table 1. Average plating thickness was 13 μm (0.0005

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inch). Specimens were not baked after being plated.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Hydrogen embrittlement testing was done by recording time to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: failure of HEP embrittlement test strips (Luster-On Products, Inc)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which had a stress applied to them by bending and placing in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Lucite fixture within 1 hour after plating.6. These strips were shown

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to be very sensitive to hydrogen embrittlement and also repro-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ducible in a previous study on porous Cd plating.6 Corrosion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: behavior was evaluated using the salt spray test (ASTM method

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: B-117) and a galvanic couple test. AISI 4130 steel sheet was utilized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for both types of tests. In the galvanic couple test, Ti-Cd plated steel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was coupled to either Al 2024-T851 or Al 7075-T7651 alloys in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3.5% NaCl for a period of 24 hours. The Cd dissolution rate was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: calculated by weighing the Cd/steel sample before and after the test

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to 0.1 mg and dividing by the geometric area and time of test. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: average galvanic current density

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was calculated by dividing the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: average galvanic current

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: obtained by integration of the galvanic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: current-time trace) by the geometric area of the Cd/steel specimen.
